notes:
I was able to read only about 20 pages before the research tools hit their usage limit. So these notes are uneven: verses 1–8 and 14 are well covered, and verses 9–13 have less. Everything below is my own summary of pages I actually read. Gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Background

- Paul probably wrote around AD 57, when Nero was emperor. Christians were viewed with suspicion, but the worst persecutions hadn't started yet. https://biblehub.com/romans/13.htm
- Gill says Christians were accused of stirring up trouble, partly because many were Jews who resented Roman rule and Roman taxes. Paul wanted the Roman believers to set a loyal example. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- Wesley says Paul writes so much about rulers because Rome was the seat of the empire. The passage also worked as a public defence of the Christian faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- The ICC commentary says one theme running through these chapters is peace in every relationship. The teaching on rulers matches Jesus' teaching in Matthew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/icc/romans/13.htm

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Link to ch. 12:** Christians must not take personal revenge (12:19), but that doesn't cancel the state's right to punish. "Everyone" includes believers. It also stands against zealous Jews of the time who would accept no king but God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Not always a blessing:** Guzik says God sometimes appoints leaders to judge a nation rather than bless it. Paul wrote this under a Roman Empire that was no friend to Christians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Government vs. its form:** Gill says government itself is God's order, but the form (monarchy and so on) is a human choice. Some rulers seize power or abuse it. God permits this but doesn't approve it. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Who must submit:** Gill says "every soul" means every person, clergy included. He adds that the pope is not exempt. Rulers' power reaches the body and civil life, not the conscience in matters of religion. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **The office, not each ruler:** Chrysostom asks whether every ruler is chosen by God. He answers that Paul means the institution of rule itself, because disorder and anarchy are evils. Apostles, prophets, priests and monks must submit too. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210223.htm
- **Wesley:** rulers act as God's deputies, so their authority calls for obedience from conscience. God set up government in general and permits each ruler by his providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/13.htm
- **Greek and other older notes:** The Biblehub 13:1 page collects several older commentaries.
  - The Greek perfect tense means the arrangement was set up and is still in force.
  - One note says every kind of government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) is as truly God's appointment as Israel's was.
  - Another says the believer submitting to even an unjust ruler is ultimately obeying God's will.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/13-1.htm
- **Utley (bible.org):** "authorities" here means civil rulers, not the spiritual powers the same Greek word refers to elsewhere. The verse teaches God's will for order, not the "divine right of kings." https://bible.org/book/export/html/21373

**v. 2**
- **Resisting God:** Since government's authority comes from God, believers must obey unless told to sin. In that case Acts 4:19 applies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Whose judgment:** JFB says the "condemnation" comes from God, whose authority is being resisted through the ruler. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/romans-13.html
- **Wesley adds:** the condemnation comes from God as well as from the magistrate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **Cambridge Bible:** even at its worst, civil authority is far better than anarchy. It never systematically rewards wrong as wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/romans/13.htm
- **Utley:** the Greek suggests a settled, personal habit of rebellion against established order. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21373

**v. 3**
- **Good citizens:** Christians should be the best citizens. They are honest, pay taxes and pray for rulers, though their first loyalty is to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** "good works" here means good behaviour as citizens. Good subjects also gain their rulers' protection. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Wesley:** rulers are generally a terror only to evil, though there are exceptions. He separates two fears. One comes before wrongdoing and holds us back, and it should stay. The other follows wrongdoing, and those who do right are free of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **Sproul's Ligonier devotional:** the believer's instinct should be to obey. Any decision to disobey should come only after much prayer. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servant-our-good

**v. 4**
- **"God's minister":** officials have a role in God's plan just as church leaders do. They should remember they are servants, not gods. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **The sword (Guzik):** the sword stands for capital punishment, since Rome usually executed by beheading. Paul does not doubt the state's right to execute. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **The sword (others):** Wesley and Gill also read it as the power of life and death. Gill says it covers all lawful punishments, and rulers ought to use it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html ; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Why government is good (Gill):** it protects life, holds back vice, encourages virtue and defends against foreign enemies. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Calvin:** the magistrate's vengeance is God's vengeance, carried out through human servants. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/institutes.vi.xxi.html
- **TGC essay:** governments hold "the power of the sword" and churches "the power of the keys." Neither may force true worship, and the state may not criminalise every sin. The authority goes back to Genesis 9 and sets up no particular form of government. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-relationship-of-church-and-state/

**v. 5**
- **Not blind obedience:** Guzik says obedience for conscience' sake keeps the eyes of conscience open. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Calvin:** subjects shouldn't obey merely from fear, as people submit to an armed enemy. Their obedience is really given to God. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/institutes.vi.xxi.html
- **Wesley:** "wrath" means human punishment, and "conscience" means obedience to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **JFB:** this applies to every form of government, from Nero's despotism to pure democracy. Citizens' right to work to change or improve their government is "left untouched." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/romans-13.html
- **ICC:** early Christians obeyed in all matters of indifference. They disobeyed only when conscience required it and never encouraged rebellion. Church and state are separate spheres. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/icc/romans/13.htm

**v. 6**
- **Taxes:** paying them supports God's work in a sense. The verse implies taxes are for restraining evil and keeping order, not for making officials rich. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** governing takes much care and expense, so taxes should be paid cheerfully. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Ligonier:** taxes must be paid even when the rate is a burden or unjust. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/civil-disobedience-2

**v. 7**
- **Wesley's definitions:** "tribute" is tax on persons or property, "custom" is duty on goods, "fear" is obedience and "honour" is reverence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **Gill:** good subjects don't need to fear punishment. The "fear" here is reverence and fear of giving offence. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Caesar and God:** give the state what is due while keeping for God what belongs to him alone (Matthew 22:21). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/

**v. 8**
- **Love as a debt:** love is the one debt that is never paid off. Guzik says this verse does not ban borrowing, since Jesus allowed it (Matthew 5:42), though Proverbs 22:7 warns of its dangers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** money debts are included. Debt can't always be avoided, but running up debt carelessly is a disgrace to the gospel. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Living by Faith commentary (StudyLight):** you only "owe" in this verse's sense when you miss payments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/13-8.html
- **Wesley:** love is an eternal debt. If it is paid properly, it pays all the others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/13.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** the perfect tense shows that love in principle fulfils the commandments about our neighbour all at once. Here "the law" means only those commandments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/romans/13.htm

**v. 9**
- **Gill:** Paul lists commandments from the second table of the law (duties to others) to show that love keeps them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/romans-13.html
- **Wesley:** if your heart is full of love, you keep the commandments even without thinking about them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **Echo of Jesus:** this repeats Jesus' words in Matthew 22:36–40. Loving your neighbour means real people you meet every day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/

**v. 10**
- **Wesley:** the love that keeps us from all evil also moves us to all good. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **Guzik:** love is the true measure of our obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/

**v. 11**
- **Wesley:** "do this" means keep the law of love. The time is "full of grace, but hasting away." Night stands for this life and day for the resurrection, and the salvation that is "nearer" is final salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html ; https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/
- **Guzik:** Christ's return is near. You can do many religious things while being "asleep" towards God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** God wakes sleeping believers gently by his love, through rebukes in preaching, or through persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **ICC:** asks how much of this comes from Jesus' own teaching that his coming would be real and sudden. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/icc/romans/13.htm

**v. 12**
- **Clothing picture:** taking off old clothes and putting on new ones. You must take off sin's rags before putting on Christ (Guzik, quoting Spurgeon). The "armour of light" is closely tied to Christ himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/

**v. 13**
- **JFB:** people choose night for their parties, but believers' night is over. The three pairs of sins are kinds of excess, kinds of sexual impurity, and kinds of hostility that reverse the law of love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/romans-13.html
- **Word meanings (Guzik):** "licentiousness" suggests desire for a forbidden bed. "Lust" describes people with no shame left. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** groups the sins as against sobriety, chastity and peace. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm

**v. 14**
- **Augustine:** this verse led to his conversion (Precept Austin quotes him, and Guzik mentions it too). https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_13_notes_pt3 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **"Make no provision":** Christ works through us as we actively cooperate. He doesn't do it for us while we sit back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- **Gill:** caring for the body is fine; feeding its lusts is not. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- **Wesley:** "Herein is contained the whole of our salvation." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 1–2, 5: Can Christians ever resist the state?**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** you cannot resist the magistrate without resisting God. Private people should not interfere in public affairs. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/institutes.vi.xxi.html (I couldn't read his later sections, often cited, on "lesser magistrates" resisting tyrants.)
- **Ligonier (Reformed, today):** Christians must disobey when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. Corrupt rulers are not to be dealt with outside the law. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/obedience-civil-authorities ; https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/civil-obedience-2/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/civil-disobedience-2
- **Wesley (Methodist):** forbids resistance "in any other manner than the laws of the community direct." That suggests lawful means of opposition are allowed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html
- **One older note on Biblehub's 13:1 page:** the verse concerns the form of government, not every person who holds power. A ruler who destroys a nation's basic laws "is not from God" and may be resisted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/13-1.htm
- **JFB:** citizens may work to change their government. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/romans-13.html
- **Guzik (enduringword.com, which falls under your Pentecostal/charismatic group):** in a democracy citizens in a sense *are* the government and should take part. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/

**vv. 1–4: Lutheran "two kingdoms" vs. a Baptist alternative**
- **LCMS:** Luther saw government as God's tool for keeping outward peace. It makes no one righteous before God. Christians live under it to serve their neighbour. https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/books-essays-articles/kingdom-of-the-left-luther-on-temporal-authority/
- **1517.org:** two kingdoms is a form of Lutheran Law-and-Gospel teaching. God rules the "left-hand" kingdom by law and the sword, and the church should not run worldly government. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-romans-131-10-pentecost-15-series-a-2023
- **LCMS President Harrison:** the state is ruled by reason and the church by the Word. Both belong to God. https://reporter.lcms.org/2016/president-harrison-provides-a-lutheran-view-of-church-and-state?amp=&amp=&amp=
- **Jonathan Leeman (TGC, Baptist):** he finds Luther's scheme forced. He proposes "two ages" instead: Caesar is honoured because his sword makes space for the gospel, not because he can save. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/not-two-kingdoms-but-two-ages/

**v. 8: Does "owe no one" forbid debt?**
- Guzik says no (see v. 8 above). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-13/
- Gill (a Baptist) treats careless debt as shameful. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm
- The Living by Faith commentary says it is only sin when payments are missed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/13-8.html

**v. 10: How fully can love keep the law?**
- **Gill:** no one keeps it perfectly. Only Christ fulfilled the law perfectly, and we look to him for our righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/13-8.html
- **Cambridge Bible:** Paul is stating the ideal, not denying that believers fall short. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/romans/13.htm
- **Wesley:** stresses the positive power of a heart full of love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-13.html

**v. 14: Putting on Christ: justification or daily living?**
- One writer quoted by Precept Austin says we don't put on Christ as our righteousness, but for our "walk and warfare."
- Another says it happens in two ways: once as the robe of righteousness when we believe, and again as daily armour.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_13_notes_pt3
- Wesley calls it the whole of salvation. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/

---

## Other views

- **Catholic and Orthodox (Chrysostom, honoured by both):** see v. 1. He also says submitting to rulers is really submitting to God, so believers need not feel lowered by it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210223.htm
- **Catholic vs. Protestant contrast:** both Chrysostom and Gill say clergy are under civil authority. Gill specifically aims this at the pope's claims. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/13.htm

So these notes have no modern-scholarship section, no Orthodox source beyond Chrysostom, and nothing on popular modern teaching. The Pentecostal voice is only Guzik, and Anglican voices aren't clearly identified. A further session could fill those gaps.
